studies.name: HyTEC overview: high dose per fraction hypofractionated treatment effects
studies.tldr: 7 NTCP and 9 TCP papers across 6 anatomic sites: AAPM pools SRS/SBRT dose-volume-outcome data, adding tumor control to QUANTEC-style toxicity estimates.
details: 🔍 AAPM WGSBRT literature-pooling initiative; reports published in the Red Journal by AAPM/ASTRO agreement

Constraints mostly assume an unirradiated field, so reirradiation and pediatric cases need the organ-specific papers.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Literature pooling by the **AAPM WGSBRT** within the Biological Effects Sub-Committee, using publications with a minimal data set (dose schedule, prescription practice, critical-structure dose, outcome). Output: **7 NTCP and 9 TCP papers** across 6 sites, plus vision papers on immunomodulation, indirect cell death and modelling.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **NTCP** (organ-specific toxicity) and **TCP**, mostly 1-5 year local control. Clinical values were preferred over model-based estimates where both existed.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Successor to **Emami et al** and **QUANTEC**, both built mainly for conventional fractionation and, for QUANTEC, focused on NTCP. HyTEC adds **tumor control**, and sits alongside AAPM TG-101 SBRT constraints rather than replacing them.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents adults treated with SRS/SBRT/SABR, with NTCP entries mostly for pts without prior RT. Does not represent children (PENTEC) or most reirradiation scenarios.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Source series are mostly retrospective, with inconsistent dose specification, segmentation and outcome definitions. Pooling across schedules relies on the **linear-quadratic model**, which the authors call simplistic, and imaging-defined local recurrence plus favorable selection may inflate TCP.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The authors argue dose-volume-outcome reporting has **not improved enough since QUANTEC** to support clean pooling. Their remedy is discrete capture via EHRs, planning systems, CTCAE grading, TG-263 naming and contouring atlases, an infrastructure argument rather than a result.

studies.interpretation:
HyTEC is best read as the SBRT-era counterpart to QUANTEC rather than as new evidence. Its value is consolidation: it takes a literature that grew quickly and unevenly and turns it into dose-volume-outcome tables a planner can consult. Emami et al offered uniform TD 5/5 and TD 50/5 estimates for partial and whole organ irradiation, drawn largely from expert opinion, and QUANTEC moved to organ-specific dose-volume metrics from CT-era data. HyTEC's main conceptual addition is pairing tumor control with toxicity. That pairing matters for SBRT in particular, because the case for high dose per fraction has rested on local control, and a constraint table with no control table invites a planner to trade away the effect that justified the technique.

How much confidence a reader places in any entry should depend on how it was generated. The authors pooled published reports that met a minimal data threshold and preferred clinical over modelled values. Even so, the underlying series are mostly retrospective, dose specification and segmentation vary across institutions, and pooling across schedules leans on the linear-quadratic model, which the authors themselves call simplistic at these doses. On the TCP side the bias runs in one direction. Actuarial local control that censors at death, in a population where systemic progression and local regrowth are probably linked, will tend to overstate control, and so will imaging-based calls of recurrence and favorable selection. Treat the TCP estimates as upper bounds for an unselected metastatic population.

On the NTCP side the practical boundary is prior RT. Most entries assume an unirradiated field, and the footnotes flag specific interactions, such as prior whole-brain RT raising brainstem risk with later SRS. Short survival among many SBRT pts also means late toxicity may be undercounted. That cuts against leaning on these values for oligometastatic or curative-intent pts who will live long enough to express late effects.

Several of the most transferable details sit in footnotes rather than headline values. For spine, a minimum tumor dose or GTV D95 may predict control better than the nominal prescription, which moves attention from the prescription to target coverage. For prostate, the pooled series often used heterogeneous plans with a mean prescription isodose of 85%, so the reported toxicity came with intentional intraprostatic hot spots. A homogeneous plan to the same prescription is a different treatment, and borrowing the constraints without the dose distribution is an extrapolation.

What HyTEC does not settle is whether these estimates hold prospectively. The authors' own conclusion is that reporting has not improved enough since QUANTEC to allow cleaner pooling. Their proposed remedy, discrete capture from EHRs, planning systems and standardized toxicity grading, is an argument about infrastructure, not a finding. Pediatric pts are out of scope and deferred to PENTEC.

Reirradiation and pediatric cases need the organ-specific papers.

studies.monday_clinic: In SLN-negative, LVSI-negative FIGO 2009 stage IB grade 3 endometrioid disease, this talk's framework assigns pelvic EBRT delivered with IMRT; it does not address molecularly classified or non-endometrioid stage I disease.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: **Pelvic EBRT** for stage IB grade III and stage II (plus **vaginal cuff brachy boost** for stage II); vaginal cuff brachy alone for stage IA grade III or IB grade I-II. IMRT favored over 3D conformal on TIME-C bowel PROs.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: HIR thresholds come from GOG99, PORTEC-1, PORTEC-2 and GOG249, which use **different age cut points and factor counts**. Stage III-IV options are listed without the randomized chemoRT-vs-chemo trials that frame that choice.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents surgically staged early-stage endometrioid endometrial cancer under FIGO 2009. Does not represent molecularly classified disease or serous / clear cell histology, which the algorithm does not separate.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: A teaching grid that compresses the PORTEC/GOG-era consensus into one table. The **stage IB grade 3** assignment and the absence of molecular class are where a current reader would most need to overlay newer data.

studies.interpretation:
This deck is a teaching framework rather than new evidence, and its value is compression: one grid that maps FIGO 2009 stage, grade and histology onto observation, vaginal cuff brachytherapy, pelvic EBRT, or combined therapy. That grid reflects the consensus built through the PORTEC and GOG trials, in which adjuvant pelvic RT reduced pelvic recurrence in intermediate-risk disease without a convincing survival gain, and PORTEC-2 then moved most high-intermediate pts from pelvic EBRT to vaginal brachytherapy alone.

The weakest join is the cell the case lands in. Stage IB grade 3 endometrioid disease is assigned pelvic EBRT, yet the PORTEC-2 definition reproduced on the slide excludes grade 3 with >1/2 invasion, so the trial that legitimized brachytherapy alone never tested this patient. The HIR slide also shows that high-intermediate risk is not one population: GOG99, PORTEC-1, PORTEC-2 and GOG249 each draw the line with different age cut points and factor counts, so a patient can be HIR under one definition and not another. GOG249, which tested pelvic RT against vaginal brachytherapy plus chemotherapy in early high-intermediate and high-risk disease, is listed only for its definition; its result is the comparison most relevant to this case and is not on the slides.

The larger gap is molecular. The deck carries Type I/II histology and mentions TP53 and MMR biology in passing, but the algorithm does not use them. Molecular class (POLE-mutant, MMRd, TP53-abnormal, no specific molecular profile) now reassigns adjuvant intensity in exactly this stage I grade 3 group, with POLE-mutant tumors candidates for de-escalation and TP53-abnormal tumors for escalation, and later staging revisions fold that biology into the stage itself. A reader applying this grid today would need to overlay molecular class before choosing between brachytherapy, pelvic EBRT, and systemic therapy.

The technique slide is the most transferable piece. TIME-C is a randomized comparison, and its patient-reported bowel endpoints at 5 weeks favor IMRT for pelvic fields, which is the argument for IMRT whenever pelvic EBRT is chosen. The 1 yr diarrhea line, though, is printed as p=0.4 while being listed among the IMRT reductions; that is either a slide typo or a nonsignificant difference, and it should be checked against the primary report before being cited. The follow-up schedule and dilator guidance are practical but rest on practice convention rather than trial data, and the talk presents them as such.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: The stage IB grade 3 cell assigned pelvic EBRT sits outside PORTEC-2, which excluded grade 3 with >1/2 invasion, so no randomized brachy-vs-EBRT data back it here. When pelvic fields are used, TIME-C bowel PROs (diarrhea at 5 weeks 33.7% vs 51.9%) favor IMRT over 3D.

presentation.speaker: Justin Anderson, MD
presentation.summary: The speaker walks a stage IB grade 3 endometrioid case through workup, surgical staging and adjuvant selection. The framework assigns adjuvant therapy by FIGO 2009 stage, grade and histology: observation for low-grade stage IA without LVSI, vaginal cuff brachytherapy for intermediate cells, pelvic EBRT for stage IB grade 3, and EBRT plus brachy boost for stage II. High-intermediate risk is defined through the competing GOG99, PORTEC-1, PORTEC-2 and GOG249 criteria. For pelvic fields the talk argues IMRT over 3D, resting on RTOG 1203 (TIME-C) patient-reported bowel outcomes.
critique: The algorithm runs on FIGO 2009 stage, grade and Type I/II histology; molecular class (POLE, MMRd, TP53-abnormal) does not enter, though it now shifts adjuvant intensity in exactly the stage I grade 3 cell the case occupies.
Stage IB grade 3 is assigned pelvic EBRT, but the PORTEC-2 definition on the slide excludes grade 3 with >1/2 invasion, so the talk offers no randomized brachy-vs-EBRT data for its own case.

GOG249 appears only as an HIR definition; its comparison of pelvic RT against vaginal brachy plus chemo, the data closest to this case, is not presented, and the four HIR definitions shown disagree on who qualifies.
The TIME-C slide lists diarrhea at 1 yr (5.8% vs 15.1%, p=0.4) among IMRT reductions; as printed that difference is nonsignificant, so either the slide carries a typo or the claim overreaches.

sites.intro: Two HyTEC SRS tolerance papers; optic limits hold only without prior RT, and no NTCP model was possible after prior RT.

studies.name: HyTEC: SRS dose/volume tolerances of the brain
studies.tldr: Brain mets: 1fx V12 (incl. target) 5/10/>15 cc → ~10%/15%/20% symptomatic RN; 3fx V18 <30 cc and V23 <7 cc → <10%.

details.text: 📊 1fx SRS for brain mets: symptomatic RN by V12 (including target volume)

details: 📊 3fx fSRS for brain mets: normal-brain V18 <30 cc and V23 <7 cc → <10% RN risk
📊 AVM SRS: modestly lower symptomatic RN than brain mets at equivalent V12

details.text: 📐 Pooled NTCP model parameters (single-fraction equivalent, α/β=2 Gy)

details: 🔍 AAPM HyTEC pooled review: 51 reports, 9,828 pts, 13,913 targets (~7,814 unique pts)
🔍 NTCP modelling limited to 5 studies with per-target dose, volume and outcome
🔍 Excluded cohorts made up solely of glioma, meningioma, vestibular schwannoma or brainstem targets

details.text: 🔗 RTOG 90-05 (recurrent, previously irradiated mets + gliomas): crude G≥3 neurotoxicity by diameter

details: 🔗 Cleveland Clinic (896 pts, 3,034 mets ≤2 cm): >1 cm → 2.1-fold necrosis, 4.8-fold symptomatic necrosis
⚠️ Crude, not actuarial, risks; median RN onset roughly a year after SRS/fSRS
⚠️ RN vs progression: imaging sensitivity ~60–80%; most diagnoses imaging-only

verdict.rationale: Pooled retrospective crude rates; heterogeneous endpoints and volume definitions (tissue vs brain Vx); RN rarely path-confirmed. Models partly descriptive, not validated predictors.
verdict.audience: Brain mets or AVM treated with 1-5 fraction SRS/fSRS

studies.significance: The thresholds use V12 including target, and definitions diverge: for a 2.5 cm target, brain V12 7.4 cc vs tissue V12 15.6 cc in the authors' example. A brain-minus-GTV readout run against these numbers understates exposure, and on the steep part of the curve about 1 cc of volume uncertainty moves risk by about 5%.
studies.monday_clinic: In a brain met whose single-fraction plan carries a V12 including target of 10 cc or more, this pooled data puts symptomatic RN at roughly 15% to 20% and supports fractionated SRS as the lower-risk option; it does not extend to brainstem targets or glioma.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: AAPM HyTEC working group pooled review of PubMed reports 1995-2016 plus one 2018 study: **51 reports**, 9,828 pts and 13,913 targets, ~7,814 unique pts after overlap. NTCP models were fit only to the **5 studies** reporting per-target dose, volume and outcome.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Mostly AVM (an estimated 3,848 pts with 3,858 AVMs) and brain mets (3,966 pts with 7,903 mets). Cohorts made up **solely** of glioma, meningioma (edema), vestibular schwannoma or brainstem targets were excluded. 10 studies included SRS to a resection cavity.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: Single-fraction SRS and 2-5 fraction fSRS (GK and CK in the modelled series). Multi-fraction doses converted to single-fraction equivalent with LQ, **α/β=2 Gy**.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: Heterogeneous: any RN, symptomatic RN, edema, neurologic complications, and **G3 pathologically confirmed necrosis**. Crude rather than actuarial risks used throughout.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: fSRS **appears to reduce RN risk for larger treatment volumes** relative to SRS. AVM ran modestly lower than brain mets at equivalent V12.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Single-institution series (Flickinger, Korytko, Blonigen, Minniti, Sneed) each tied V10-V12 to necrosis; this pools them and adds fSRS models. RTOG 90-05 set dose by lesion diameter, which HyTEC replaces with **normal-tissue dose-volume**.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents brain mets or AVM treated with 1-5 fraction SRS/fSRS, with V12 read as including the target. Does not represent brainstem targets, glioma, meningioma or vestibular schwannoma.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Bin medians were estimated from bin midpoints, and V10/V14 were converted to V12. Korytko's risks ran **substantially higher** than other series and were modelled separately. Vx was per lesion in some series and per patient in others.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: Risk rises continuously with dose-volume rather than at a single threshold, so the volume definition on the planning readout matters as much as the number. Standardized dosimetric and toxicity reporting is the stated prerequisite for refining these models.

studies.interpretation:
The practical value of this report is that it turns a set of loosely compatible single-institution series into a dose-volume vocabulary a planner can use. The abstract's single-fraction anchors (V12 including target of 5, 10 and >15 cc mapping to roughly 10%, 15% and 20% symptomatic radionecrosis) are what most clinics will carry away. They sit comfortably beside the Flickinger and Korytko work that first tied V10 to V12 exposure to necrosis, and they finish moving the field away from the RTOG 90-05 habit of setting dose by lesion diameter. What the report adds over those series is the multi-fraction side: 3-fraction normal-brain constraints of V18 <30 cc and V23 <7 cc, and the authors' conclusion that fractionation appears to lower risk once treatment volumes get large.

Confidence should be tempered by how the data were assembled. Risks are crude, not actuarial, in a population where median time to necrosis is roughly a year and many pts with brain mets do not live through that window. Crude rates in a short-survival cohort will understate the risk carried by a long survivor, and long survivors are exactly the pts in whom necrosis costs the most. Bin medians were estimated from midpoints, V10 and V14 were converted to V12, and the endpoint ranged from any imaging change to pathologically confirmed G3 necrosis. The authors call several fitted curves descriptive rather than predictive. The largest outlier, Korytko, ran substantially higher than the other series and had to be modelled separately, which suggests that in places the spread between studies is as large as the dose-volume effect being estimated.

The diagnostic problem cuts both ways. Imaging sensitivity for separating necrosis from progression sits on the order of 60-80%, and few series had pathology. Some events counted as necrosis are tumor, and some progression calls are necrosis. This report cannot tell you which direction the net bias runs, and that uncertainty widens as immunotherapy changes the imaging appearance of both.

The volume definition is the quieter trap. Series reported tissue, normal-tissue or brain Vx, and some counted per lesion while others counted per patient. A clinic that applies the single-fraction thresholds to a brain-minus-GTV metric, or to a per-lesion volume in a multi-met plan, is applying a constraint to a quantity the model was not fit on.

What this leaves open: whether the curves hold for resection-cavity SRS, which only a minority of series addressed; whether concurrent immunotherapy shifts risk at a given V12; and how far the fSRS models generalize, since the pooled multi-fraction modelling rests largely on the Inoue and Peng series. The report is best read as a calibration of current practice rather than new evidence that should move it, and as an argument that dose-volume and toxicity reporting has to be standardized before the next pooled analysis can do better.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: The thresholds use V12 including target, and for a 2.5 cm target brain V12 7.4 cc vs tissue V12 15.6 cc in the authors' example. A brain-minus-GTV readout understates exposure, and on the steep part of the curve about 1 cc of volume uncertainty moves risk by about 5%.

studies.name: HyTEC: SRS dose tolerances of the optic pathways
studies.tldr: <1% RION at optic apparatus max point dose 10 Gy/1 fx, 20 Gy/3 fx, 25 Gy/5 fx in pts without prior RT; 34 studies, 1,578 pts.
details: 📊 <1% RION at max point dose 10 Gy/1 fx, 20 Gy/3 fx, 25 Gy/5 fx (no prior RT)

details.text: 📊 Calculated NTCP tolerance doses, optic apparatus max point dose, no prior RT (Table 3)

details: 🔍 Pooled analysis of published reports: 34 studies, 1,578 pts, PubMed 1990 to Jun 2015 (AAPM WGSBRT)

details.text: 📊 Crude RION rates by era and prior RT
subdetails: 1997+ studies, no prior RT: <1% (9 of 1224)
1997+ SRS 9 of 959 vs fSRS 1 of 265, p=0.7
1997+ studies, prior RT: 11% (7 of 61), p<0.00001 vs no prior RT
Pre-1997 studies, no prior RT: 8.5%; 3.6% excluding the VEP-endpoint study (p=0.002 vs 1997+)

details: 📐 KM stratified at 12 Gy single-fraction (EQD2 45.3 Gy, α/β 1.6): lower RION risk below 12 Gy
🔗 vs QUANTEC: RION negligible below 8 Gy single-fraction max dose, rising to 10% at 12-15 Gy
⚠️ Non-event doses mostly reported only as medians or quartiles; likelihood fit may overweight events
⚠️ RION definitions varied; Leber's VEP-inclusive endpoint gave 23% at median max dose ~15 Gy
⚠️ No NTCP model possible after prior RT: too few pts, events, and details

verdict.rationale: Aggregate published-report data; non-event doses mostly medians, RION definitions heterogeneous, and multi-fraction limits depend on α/β 1.6 conversion from sparse fSRS events.
verdict.audience: Peri-optic skull base tumors, 1-5 fx SRS/fSRS, no prior RT

studies.significance: The single-fraction-only fit is the conservative read: 1% RION at 10.0 Gy and 5% at 14.0 Gy max point dose, against 12.1 Gy for 1% once fSRS series are pooled in. The 3- and 5-fraction limits (20 and 25 Gy) rest on 265 fSRS pts with 1 event, converted at α/β 1.6, so they gate peri-optic fSRS planning less firmly than the single-fraction number.
studies.monday_clinic: In peri-optic pituitary adenoma, cavernous sinus meningioma or craniopharyngioma without prior RT, this supports SRS or 2-5 fx fSRS within the HyTEC point-dose limits at <1% RION risk; it does not extend to re-irradiation, where crude RION was 11% and no NTCP model could be fit.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Pooled analysis of published reports (PubMed 1990 to Jun 2015) from the AAPM Working Group on Stereotactic Body Radiotherapy: **34 studies, 1,578 pts**. Max dose known for every RION event, but non-event doses mostly available only as medians or quartiles. **Probit NTCP model** fit to 1997+ studies, no prior RT.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Pituitary adenoma, cavernous sinus meningioma, craniopharyngioma and malignant skull base tumors after SRS or 2-5 fx fSRS. Excluded optic nerve sheath tumors, optic gliomas, ocular/uveal melanoma, and studies not separating tumor progression from RION. **Prior resection 76%**, **prior RT 6%**.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: Dose metric is **optic apparatus maximum point dose**, generally a small volume (<0.035 cc per TG101). Multi-fraction doses converted at **α/β 1.6 Gy**. LINAC, Gamma Knife and CyberKnife series; delivery system showed no effect on RION.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: RION scored as loss of visual acuity, visual field change and/or blindness, using varied scales (LENT SOMA, CTCAE v3, CTCAE v4) or unspecified symptom reporting.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: In 1997+ studies without prior RT, crude RION **<1% (9 of 1224)**, with SRS 9 of 959 vs fSRS 1 of 265 (p=0.7). Prior RT: **11% (7 of 61)**, p<0.00001. Prior resection did not correlate with RION (p=0.66).

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: QUANTEC found RION negligible below **8 Gy** single-fraction max dose, rising to 10% at 12-15 Gy. HyTEC puts 1% risk at **10.0 Gy** (single-fraction model) or **12.1 Gy** (all studies), modestly more permissive. Mayo's >300-pt no-prior-RT experience had 1 RION event, at 12.8 Gy.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents pts with peri-optic skull base tumors and no prior RT receiving 1-5 fx SRS or fSRS. Does not represent re-irradiation, primary optic nerve or orbital tumors, or stereotactic RT beyond 5 fractions.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: The 1997 era split was chosen after inspecting the data to isolate early high-toxicity studies. Planning-system dose calculations may differ by ~10%, optic apparatus contouring varies, and subjective symptom capture likely undercounts RION. Dose-volume data were too sparse to model.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: Supports a single-fraction point limit near **10 Gy** rather than a strict 8 Gy cap when target coverage is at stake. The multi-fraction limits are less certain, and volume dependence is open: a Mayo series of 133 pts with no RION had median volumes above 10 and 12 Gy of 1.6 and 0.1 mm3.

studies.interpretation:
The practical question this paper answers is how far a radiosurgeon has to hold the optic apparatus away from a peri-optic target. The long-standing reference was QUANTEC: negligible risk under 8 Gy in a single fraction, climbing to 10% in the 12-15 Gy range, and several institutions adopted 8 Gy as their working cap. HyTEC's pooled estimate is more permissive, placing 1% RION at 10.0 Gy when the model uses single-fraction data alone and at 12.1 Gy when hypofractionated series are folded in. For a meningioma lying against the chiasm, the difference between an 8 Gy and a 10 Gy point limit can decide whether the target is covered or a sliver is deliberately underdosed, so the direction of the revision matters more than its size.

How much confidence to place in these numbers depends on which number. The single-fraction estimate draws on most of the data and involves no dose conversion; the Mayo experience of more than 300 pts without prior RT, with one event at 12.8 Gy, is consistent with it. The 3- and 5-fraction limits are weaker. They come from 265 fSRS pts with 1 event, and they are reached through an α/β of 1.6 Gy, so a reader skeptical of the LQ model in the stereotactic range should treat 20 Gy in 3 fractions and 25 Gy in 5 as extrapolations rather than observations. That the all-studies fit is more permissive than the single-fraction fit suggests the converted multi-fraction data move the curve, and the conservative fit is the one with less modelling between dose and event.

The method carries a structural bias the authors name themselves. Every RION event arrives with its own maximum dose, but most pts without an event appear only as a cohort median or quartile. A likelihood fit cannot see that some non-event pts sat near the event doses, so it overweights the events and returns a conservative curve; the inverse-variance alternative trades that bias for lost dose resolution. Add heterogeneous endpoints (one series using visual evoked potentials reported 23%), inconsistent contouring of a structure a few millimetres across, planning-system dose differences of perhaps 10%, and largely subjective symptom capture likely to miss events, and the curves are best read as an envelope rather than a dose-response measured in any single cohort.

The era split does more work than it first appears to. Pre-1997 studies had a crude RION rate of 8.5% without prior RT, against under 1% in later series, and the boundary was drawn after looking at the data to separate the early high-toxicity reports. The modern-era model is the relevant one for current practice, but it also inherits whatever selection put the early studies on the wrong side of that line. Delivery platform made no difference, which supports carrying the limits across Gamma Knife, CyberKnife and LINAC practice.

What the paper leaves untouched is the patient who most needs a number. Prior RT carried an 11% crude rate (7 of 61) against under 1% without it, and the data were too thin to fit any model. Volume effects are also unresolved: the Mayo parasellar series found very small volumes above 10 and 12 Gy (1.6 and 0.1 mm3) on sides that never developed RION, hinting that a small hot spot may be tolerable, but nothing here quantifies that. For re-irradiation and for dose-volume constraints, this analysis is a starting point, not an answer.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: The single-fraction-only fit is the conservative read: 1% RION at 10.0 Gy and 5% at 14.0 Gy max point dose, against 12.1 Gy once fSRS series are pooled in. The 20 and 25 Gy multi-fraction limits rest on 265 fSRS pts with 1 event, converted at α/β 1.6.

studies.name: Genomic testing for therapy selection in prostate cancer (Feng)
studies.tldr: Decipher and PAM50 subtyping may select who needs ADT with salvage RT or gains more from apalutamide; prospective NRG trials now test this.
details: 🔍 Framework: genomic classifiers flag poor-prognosis disease and are now built into phase III trials, newly diagnosed and recurrent

details.text: 📊 Pooled RTOG 92-02 / 94-13 / 99-02 (RT ± ADT): GC score independently prognostic
subdetails: Independent for DM, BF and OS when baseline clinical variables were accounted for

details: 🔍 PREDICT-RT (NRG GU009): previously untreated high-risk (NCCN), Primary Endpoint: MFS, sample size 2478

details.text: 🔍 PREDICT-RT randomizes ADT intensity within Decipher strata

details: 🔗 RTOG 9601 parent: salvage RT + bicalutamide (2 years) vs placebo, n=760, median f/u 13 years, OS HR 0.77, p=0.04

details.text: 📊 RTOG 9601 Decipher MVA (JAMA Oncology 2021): GC and treatment effect by endpoint

details: 📊 Low Decipher risk groups: smaller absolute benefit from hormone therapy with salvage RT; per-group 12-year values not in source text
📊 SPARTAN nmCRPC: 233 pts with archived samples profiled; high and low Decipher both benefited from apalutamide, high benefited more
⚠️ SPARTAN biopsy preceded randomization by median ~ 6 years
🔗 PAM50 Luminal B prostate cancers showed the greatest ADT response in matched cohorts (Zhao, JAMA Oncology 2017)

details.text: 🔍 NRG GU006: tests Luminal B as a predictive marker for apalutamide with salvage RT
subdetails: Post-RP PSA ≥0.1 and ≤1.0 ng/mL plus ≥1 risk feature
Risk features: Gleason 4+3 or greater, persistent PSA after RP, pT3
Stratified Luminal B vs non-Luminal B
Salvage RT + 6 months placebo vs salvage RT + 6 months apalutamide
Accrued faster than expected

details: ⚠️ Slides show prognostic HRs; no biomarker-by-treatment interaction test for ADT benefit in source text
studies.significance: Two RT decisions are in play: ADT duration with definitive RT, where PREDICT-RT tests intermediate-term ADT for low or intermediate Decipher, and whether to add ADT to salvage RT, where RTOG 9601 suggests smaller absolute benefit at low Decipher. Neither is settled until those trials and NRG GU006 read out.
studies.monday_clinic: In post-RP PSA recurrence going to salvage RT, a low Decipher score is evidence context for a smaller absolute hormone-therapy gain; it does not yet support shortening ADT with definitive RT for NCCN high-risk disease, which PREDICT-RT is testing.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents high-risk localized and **post-RP PSA-recurrent** prostate cancer treated with RT ± ADT, plus **nmCRPC** for apalutamide. Does not represent mHSPC, for which no biomarker results are shown on the slides.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: The prognostic layer rests on archived tissue from **RTOG 92-02, 94-13, 99-02 and 9601**, and the nmCRPC layer on **SPARTAN**. CHAARTED, TITAN, STAMPEDE, ENZAMET and ENZARAD are listed as profiled trials, with no results on the slides.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The case for Decipher as a **prognostic** tool within NCCN risk groups is strong; the case for it as a **predictive** tool for ADT is still the hypothesis that **PREDICT-RT** and **NRG GU006** are built to test.

studies.interpretation:
The talk's core move is to treat a prognostic classifier as a candidate treatment-selection tool, and the evidence shown supports the first role far better than the second. The pooled RTOG 92-02, 94-13 and 99-02 analysis and the RTOG 9601 analysis both show GC score carrying information beyond clinical variables for distant metastasis. That is the strongest layer of the argument: it comes from archived tissue of randomized trials with long follow-up, which is about as good as retrospective biomarker work gets in prostate cancer.

The step from prognosis to prediction is where a radiation oncologist should slow down. The 9601 slides frame the result as a smaller absolute benefit from hormone therapy in low Decipher groups. Any prognostic marker produces that pattern: when baseline risk is lower, the same relative effect yields a smaller absolute gain. It is a fair basis for a shared decision about omitting hormone therapy in a low-risk salvage pt, but it is not evidence that the relative effect differs by genomic risk, and the slides as captured show no interaction test. The SPARTAN analysis has the same shape: both high and low Decipher pts benefited from apalutamide, high more. In nmCRPC that ranks expected benefit; it does not identify a group to spare.

Transferability is the next question. The 9601 hormone arm was bicalutamide, not GnRH-based ADT, and the definitive-RT cohorts predate modern imaging. A low Decipher score in a pt staged with PSMA PET may not mean the same thing as one in a conventionally staged cohort, and the talk does not address that shift.

The prospective trials are the honest answer to these gaps, and the talk presents them that way. PREDICT-RT randomizes within Decipher strata in both directions, de-intensifying to intermediate-term ADT for low or intermediate scores and adding abi/apalutamide to long-term ADT for high scores, with MFS as the primary endpoint. That design tests whether the classifier can safely move the ADT duration decision with definitive RT, the RT-adjacent decision with the most toxicity at stake. NRG GU006 is more ambitious: it stratifies on a candidate predictive marker, PAM50 Luminal B, carried over from breast cancer logic, with salvage RT plus 6 months of apalutamide or placebo.

Until those trials read out, Decipher refines risk estimates within NCCN groups and informs absolute-benefit conversations, while ADT de-intensification for high-risk definitive RT stays untested. The fast GU006 accrual shows strong demand from pts and physicians for a test that lets pts skip hormones, which is exactly why the bar for calling a marker predictive should stay high.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Decipher could move two RT-adjacent calls: ADT duration with definitive RT (PREDICT-RT tests intermediate-term ADT for low or intermediate scores) and adding ADT to salvage RT (RTOG 9601, NRG GU006). Current data support risk refinement, not ADT de-intensification.
significance_by_specialty.medonc: In SPARTAN, high-Decipher nmCRPC pts gained more from apalutamide, but low-Decipher pts benefited too, so the score ranks benefit rather than excluding anyone. PREDICT-RT tests adding abi/apalutamide to long-term ADT in high-Decipher pts.

open_questions: Does low Decipher safely de-intensify ADT with definitive RT?
Does Luminal B subtype predict apalutamide benefit with salvage RT?
How do genomic classifiers perform in PSMA PET-staged pts?

presentation.speaker: Felix Feng
presentation.summary: The speaker argued that genomic classifiers, mainly Decipher, carry prognostic information beyond clinical variables across RTOG definitive-RT and salvage-RT trials and in SPARTAN, and that this should shape ADT and ARSI decisions. In RTOG 9601, low Decipher scores tracked with a smaller absolute benefit from hormone therapy with salvage RT. The framework then moves to predictive markers: PAM50 Luminal B subtype, borrowed from breast cancer, showed the greatest ADT response. The talk closed on prospective validation, with PREDICT-RT randomizing ADT intensity by Decipher score and NRG GU006 testing apalutamide with salvage RT stratified by Luminal B status.
critique: Smaller absolute ADT benefit in low-Decipher pts is what any prognostic marker produces at lower baseline risk; the slides show no treatment-by-biomarker interaction, so predictive value for ADT is not shown.
In SPARTAN, high and low Decipher pts both benefited from apalutamide, so the 233-pt analysis ranks expected benefit rather than identifying anyone to spare.
The RTOG 9601 hormone arm was bicalutamide, not GnRH-based ADT, so carrying the Decipher-guided ADT decision to modern salvage regimens is an assumption.
All validation cohorts were conventionally staged archived tissue; the talk does not address how genomic risk groups behave once PSMA PET restages pts.
